To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the duration of an interresponse interval is determined by the minimum interresponse interval that is currently in effect and (b) the probability that the current minimum interresponse interval will change is determined by the value of the minimum interresponse intervals that are not in effect.

(1) when two minimum response times are required for reinforcement, the duration of an interresponse interval approximates the shorter of the two response time requirements and (2) when the shorter of the response time requirements is longer than the average interresponse interval on the schedule, the probability of a response burst is increased.

(a) a two-component schedule of differential-reinforcemen-of-low-rate can be established, where the two components are defined by the response that initiated the interresponse time, and (b) the two components can be maintained in a steady state for long periods of time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new type of schedule of differential reinforcement of low rate.
the development of an experimental model that will permit a more detailed analysis of the discriminative properties of nonreinforcement.
the development and application of the two-component schedules of differential reinforcement of low rates (DRL) and differential reinforcement of high rates (DRH).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the two-component schedules of differential reinforcement of low rate (DRL) are not the same as a single DRL schedule, but that they are similar in some respects.
the two-component differential reinforcement of low rate schedule is a schedule of differential reinforcement of low response rate.
a response is not only reinforced, but also punished by its consequences, and that the relative effectiveness of the two effects depends on a number of factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the rate of responding is determined by a combination of the rate of reinforcement and the discriminative function of the response.

the rate of reinforcement is not the only variable determining the rate of responding, but that the pattern of the response is determined by a variety of variables, including the discriminative events that are correlated with the reinforcement.
the rate of reinforcement is not the sole factor determining the rate of response emission.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the duration of an interresponse-time is determined by both the rate at which the response occurs, and by the value of the minimum interresponse-time that is in effect at the time the response occurs.
the value of the interresponse time, t(i) (i = 1 or 2), was determined by the discriminative function of the response, R(i) (i= 1 or 1), that produced the interresponse time.
a two-component DRL schedule can be a powerful tool for studying the discriminative functions of nonreinforced and reinforced responses.
